title: Where’s the Beef?
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
Do you remember the media frenzy over lab-grown meat? Why, several years later, has it not become a supermarket staple? Erin Somers investigates with wry humor as she throws herself, and her taste buds, into exploring why cultivated meat has yet to take over the world. You’ll devour this piece.

The two of them ate with forks and knives, passing the plate, sawing off thoughtful bites. Chewing slowly. Afterward they rendered their verdicts. “I would say it is somewhere on the spectrum between a Boca Burger and McDonald’s,” Schonwald told a reporter from NBC. “The absence of fat makes a big difference. It has the texture, which I was not expecting. It was like an animal-protein cake.” Rützler noted the burger’s blandness to a reporter from Science. “There is room for improvement here,” she said. At the end of the event, roughly $150,000 worth of burger remained uneaten. But none of this stopped Post from predicting that meat cultivated in a lab would become a consumer product within the decade.

title: 20 Minutes of Exercise Is as Good as a 90-Minute Nap If You’re Sleep Deprived - Nautilus
content:
If you’ve been to college, odds are you’ve probably stayed up late studying before a big exam. It’s a risky gambit. After all, you’re trading vitally important, brain-revitalizing sleep in order to cram in a few more facts. Now a new study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences has some good news—exercise can boost your memory just as well as a nap.

Featured Video

A research team led by neurologists from McGill University in Canada recruited 54 healthy adults (between the ages of 18 and 35) and supervised them while they stayed awake for 30 hours. After a sleepless night, the participants donned EEG readers and either napped for 90 minutes or exercised on a stationary bike for 20 minutes (a control group just sat on the bike without pedaling for 20 minutes). They were then shown a series of photos and tested three days later to determine how many they remembered.

Both the exercisers and the nappers performed significantly better on the memory test than the control group—but for different reasons. According to an analysis of the EEG data, napping seemed to recharge the brain, making it more conducive to new learning. Exercise after sleep loss, on the other hand, forced the brain to use its resources more efficiently, facilitating improved neural processing. 

Read more: “When Sleep Deprivation Is an Antidepressant”

“Sleep loss affects nearly every aspect of how we think and function, but many people can’t simply stop what they’re doing and get more sleep,” study author Marc Roig of McGill University said in a statement. “Our findings show that even a brief bout of exercise may help preserve one of our most important cognitive abilities.”

According to the team, the study “underscores the brain’s remarkable adaptive capacity to maintain cognitive performance despite being sleep deprived.” And they say their findings could help those who often work nightshifts, long shifts, or are otherwise fatigued, like truck drivers, emergency responders, and healthcare workers. 

“A nap isn’t always possible in the middle of a shift,” study author Madhura Lotlikar said. “Exercise is accessible, inexpensive, and easy to implement. That makes it a promising tool to help people stay cognitively sharp when sleep is limited.”

Still, I think we can all agree that a nap would be much better.

title: How a Cowboy Rides When the Range is on Fire
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
When Rhonda MacDonald put out a plea for help on Facebook, the cowboys answered. Wildfires have been ravaging British Columbia, Canada, this summer—and when a ranch is put under evacuation, it is no easy feat to round up 150 free‑roaming cattle. The MacDonald herd was roaming a vast, 100,000‑acre expanse of Crown rangeland above the ranch, and the people of most use were those on horseback. This exhilarating piece documents the people who came to help, and honors the skills and hard‑won knowledge needed to navigate treacherous, fire‑scarred terrain to save the herd and help a neighbour in crisis.

Before the riders headed up Mimenuh Mountain, Wayne MacDonald stood in front of a whiteboard with a red Sharpie and began drawing. Not a map, exactly. More like 50 years of memory. He sketched the ridges, draws and escape routes cattle would choose under pressure. There was one thing he kept returning to: the lack of escape routes. “As far as road, there’s one in and one out.” They knew there might come a moment when staying was no longer brave – it was reckless.

title: Sean Duffy in the Real World
author: @NewYorker
content:
I am a sucker for a travel show—if it involves people going to a place and doing a thing, count me in. My current favorites include the BBC’s “Race Across the World,” in which the scenery is usually the star—last season, sweeping shots of frozen mountain vistas had me itching to book a trip to Mongolia—and “Jet Lag: The Game,” a web series that a friend of a friend got me very, very into, in which three charming American nerds and a rotating guest player turn the world into the setting for a real-life board game, or similar. Here, the scenery is less the star than the hosts and the silly challenges they take on. In one recent season, the players had to “claim” as many adjacent U.S. states as possible by, for example, sculpting a butter animal (in Iowa), drinking at a bourbon distillery (in Kentucky), or doing time-zone trivia at a Margaritaville (in any state with a Margaritaville). It is, after all, five o’clock somewhere.

You can imagine my excitement, then, when I learned about a forthcoming YouTube offering called “The Great American Road Trip.” This one promised not only travel-show vibes but, perhaps, a sprinkling of reality TV, another guilty pleasure of mine. One of the hosts, Sean Duffy, appeared, back in 1997, on the sixth season of “The Real World,” the MTV staple in which bright young things from varied backgrounds moved in together, in this case in Boston; his memorable moments included calling one castmate a bitch and dry-humping another before gyrating with a pool cue. The new show’s other host, Rachel Campos, also appeared on a season of “The Real World”; later, she and Duffy met on a spinoff, “Road Rules” (more of the same, but on a road trip), got married, and had nine children. Campos-Duffy is now a host on Fox News; Duffy, who has hosted on Fox Business and served as a congressman from Wisconsin, is currently Donald Trump’s Transportation Secretary. Indeed, it was in this capacity that he launched “The Great American Road Trip,” with a promise to inspire other families to hit the road in honor of the country’s Semiquincentennial. “Our motto is ‘To love America is to see America,’ ” Duffy said, on Fox, in May. Campos-Duffy, sitting next to him, added that, in our “PornHub world,” the show would be “really wholesome, good family stuff.” A trailer promised as much—but also some drama.

By the time Duffy spoke about it on Fox, “The Great American Road Trip” was more or less in the can, and he said that episodes would drop in June, perhaps in time for the peak of the Semiquincentennial celebrations and summer travel season. But June brought no show, and neither did July. Meanwhile, controversy swirled around the initiative. Some critics attacked it as tone-deaf, given the war in Iran and the attendant, spiralling gas prices. (Rolling Stone calculated that a Duffy-style trip this summer might cost upward of a thousand dollars in fuel alone.) Others highlighted ethical concerns: the show was funded by a namesake nonprofit that cut sponsorship deals with various major companies—the aerospace giant Boeing, the construction provider CRH, the autonomous-driving service Waymo—that fall within Duffy’s regulatory purview. The Transportation Department insisted that this was all above board, claiming, among other things, that the road trip was official business and that Duffy had folded in relevant work meetings. After the trailer met with a withering reaction, Duffy took aim at a “radical, miserable left” that, he said, didn’t like what he was doing because “it’s too wholesome. It’s too patriotic. It’s too joyful.” During a contentious hearing before the Senate Appropriations Committee, Patty Murray, a Democrat from Washington, suggested that the whole endeavor stank. Duffy shot back, “Don’t you want to celebrate America? Let’s celebrate this country. It’s our birthday.”

On Wednesday, “The Great American Road Trip” finally landed on YouTube, in six episodes of a half hour or so each. (Technically, it should have been called “The Great American Road Trips”; as officials were keen to point out, it was filmed in installments over a period of months.) At long last, it was time to tune out the naysayers and joy haters, and judge the show on the only terms that matter for a product of the Trump Administration: whether or not it’s good TV.

During Trump’s first term, in particular, the President couldn’t pass a bowel movement without pundits declaring it “made for TV.” More often than not, I found this unbearably annoying—part of a persistent media inclination to grade the optics of the things that Trump did rather than, well, the things that Trump did. But I also felt annoyance at critics who seemed to see any mention of TV in politics as tantamount to dumbing down. TV, after all, can be very good!

Embarking on “The Great American Road Trip,” I quickly started to fear that it was not very good. The first episode—a trip to see Trump at the White House, then on to Philadelphia to learn about the Liberty Bell, meet a Benjamin Franklin impersonator, and race up the “Rocky” steps—has the feel of a promotional video that one might watch in the back of a cab. Patrick—one of the Duffys’ kids, a few of whom have clearly inherited their parents’ screen chops and brightened up the show considerably—matched my energy when a producer asked if he found it cool to visit the White House, and he replied that “it’s kind of boring, because you’re just sitting there watching your parents talk.” (“What’s so good about having cheese and steak?” Patrick asks later. “You can make that at home.”)

If Episode 1 put me to sleep, Episode 2 quickly jolted me awake. Before the Duffys even leave for their destination—Boston, this time—we learn that their daughter Paloma is applying to colleges, including Harvard, which, she says, would be hard to turn down. “Well, me and Mom can say no,” Duffy replies. Cue tense music and a disquisition on the importance of Catholicism to Duffy père and mère, who are concerned that Harvard has perfected how to take “good young girls” and “corrupt their minds.” Paloma doesn’t think that this is very open-minded, and the argument continues in the car. Eventually, both are parked—Duffy has taken the kids to see the firehouse that he once inhabited on “The Real World,” where they are welcomed in by Montana, the castmate he dry-humped. But the college plot soon recommences, and the Duffys eventually speak with a Harvard chaplain who, to some extent, is able to allay their anxieties about brainwashing. (“There is a refuge, it appears, in the Catholic Church” at Harvard, Duffy reflects. Campos-Duffy admits, “I didn’t wanna like the situation as much as I did.”) By this point, I was getting a little worried about the separation of church and state. Then I remembered, with relief, that the series was funded by corporate sponsors.

There is more drama in Episode 3 (Wyoming and Montana—the state, not the castmate): the Duffys’ eldest daughter, Evita, and her husband, Michael, who has amazing eyebrows and is currently vying for Duffy’s old congressional seat, invite an ultrasound technician to their cabin to find out the sex of their unborn child; meanwhile, Patrick has to go to the hospital after collapsing with visibly agonizing stomach pain that doctors think might be appendicitis. Happily, it turns out to be constipation, much to the amusement of the rest of the family. (“I don’t want to embarrass him,” one of his sisters says, long after that horse had bolted.) The remaining episodes—a trip to Charleston, with a detour to a Boeing plant; a trip to Texas, with a detour to a CRH subsidiary; a trip to Arizona, with a ride in a Waymo—mostly settle back into the tedium of Episode 1. Perhaps most upsetting for me, the show, as a whole, never seems to figure out whether it is primarily travel or reality, or whether the scenery or the people should be the star. The creators could have done more to bring out the gorgeous landscapes that the Duffys visited; they could, at least, have fed us some dumb challenges, with alcohol or not. Ultimately, I came away with no idea who the show is supposed to be for, although, if its paltry early view count is any guide, the answer might be “no one.”

A few months ago, in anticipation of the show’s release, I watched some old episodes of “The Real World” to get in the spirit. They were extremely dated. They were also vastly more interesting than “The Great American Road Trip” would prove to be. Duffy, for his part, came across as a real jerk at times, but surprisingly charming at others, with a half-nerd, half-jock mien—sweepy hair, big glasses, a megawatt smile—that put me in mind of a Wisconsin Sam Seaborn. (Call it “The Midwest Wing.”) According to the Times, Duffy told his “Real World” castmates that he aspired to be President one day, and “The Great American Road Trip” certainly had me wondering whether the point was to promote American travel or Duffy himself. For the record, Duffy has strongly disclaimed any interest in the White House, which is, after all, just a bunch of boring grownups talking. His show—in which he does beautiful family things with his beautiful family—does feel like a shop window, though. And, even if it isn’t, it’s an interesting thought experiment to consider whether, in this media moment, it would work as one.

It’s tempting to look at Duffy’s political ascent—and Trump’s, of course—and reflect on the surprising cultural sticking power of turn-of-the-millennium-style reality TV. And so, I will. The Trump Presidency likely wouldn’t have been possible without “The Apprentice.” Duffy’s rise has been less meteoric, but his launchpad, if anything, was an even purer distillation of the genre; as my colleague Emily Nussbaum has written, “The Real World” pioneered many of reality TV’s modern tropes—the cast of strangers, the apartment as set, the confessional interviews—and cultivated a viewership that no longer saw reality TV as a “crummy stopgap” for scripted fare but the thing to watch. When I revisited the show earlier this summer, it seemed a particularly propitious moment to assert the ongoing influence of reality TV, not least in politics. Spencer Pratt, the villain from “The Hills,” was running for mayor of Los Angeles, depicting the city as a hellhole and attracting reams of media coverage. Luke Gulbranson (“Summer House”) was running for a (year-round) U.S. House seat in Minnesota. Mark Moran (“FBoy Island”) was running for Senate in Virginia.

The moment no longer seems so propitious. Moran dropped out; Gulbranson lost, as, more significantly, did Pratt, occasioning some hand-wringing about whether his supposed surge had ever been real to begin with. (In fairness, almost nothing is more reality-TV than that.) More broadly, the genre’s future, at least as conventional TV, is in doubt, in this era of social media, podcasts, and YouTube. And yet, arguably, this array has made everything into reality TV and given everyone the tools to be a star; certainly, the genre’s codes—chiefly, its obsessions with conflict and with evaluating people’s authenticity—are baked into our modern media culture. Perhaps the most reality-TV moment of the past week came when the Georgia senator Jon Ossoff mocked Trump for flying around on his plane with “Natalie,” a winking reference to a young aide who is known for her particularly obsequious devotion to the President—and as the “human printer,” because she follows him around feeding him digital content in hard-copy form. The footage was endlessly clipped and debated. Trump responded by likening Ossoff to Pee-wee Herman. The White House communications director called him “the biggest cuck loser in politics.” (Ossoff, not Herman.)

It was certainly the most reality-TV moment of the past week to involve a politician’s travel schedule. Ironically, given his impeccable credentials, Duffy’s show didn’t come close: to the extent that it trades in “authenticity,” it is of the performative, Americana-drenched variety that the word has come to signify in politics, despite bearing little relationship to what’s real; nor does the show serve up any conflict. (Aside from the Harvard row, anyway, and even that ends happily. Spoiler ahead! Paloma is pleased to be accepted to the University of Chicago.) Throughout his political career, Duffy has seemed ambivalent about his reality roots, at times dismissing them as irrelevant, and at others leaning in, as he does, explicitly, in the Boston episode of “The Great American Road Trip,” and, implicitly, in the show’s over-all orientation. He has pushed back on the idea that the show is reality TV, but not all that convincingly—you can take the star out of reality, but not reality out of the star. Maybe, if he’d more successfully kept his distance, he could just have made a great travel show—something less “Real World” and more “real world.”

Duffy, of course, might believe that this is exactly what he did. Touting the series on X, he wrote, “America isn’t something you can understand through a phone screen. You have to get out and see it.” This is fair. If his show makes a compelling case for anything, it’s less screen time. ♦

title: Is R.F.K., Jr., Winning or Losing the War on Vaccines?
author: @NewYorker
content:
A case for cautious optimism about the Trump Administration’s war on vaccines.

August 25, 2026

Photograph by Jim Watson / Getty

This month, at an Oval Office event resounding with outlandish statements, President Trump signed an executive order called “Delivering Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations for Americans.” His order cut the number of vaccines the federal government recommends for all children from seventeen to eleven. It threatened legal action against states that don’t grant expansive exemptions from vaccine mandates. And it proposed that the vaccine against measles, mumps, and rubella (M.M.R.), which is currently combined to curb costs and reduce the total number of injections that children receive, be separated into three different shots.

In his remarks, Trump repeated a debunked theory that vaccines are linked to rising autism rates. He claimed, incorrectly, that doctors were injecting doses “the size of a bottle of soda” into tiny bodies, and argued that the M.M.R. shot “can be explosive” and “quite lethal.” (M.M.R. vaccines have been administered hundreds of millions of times, and have contributed to saving millions of lives while causing meaningful side effects in only the tiniest minority of cases.) During the event, he made sure to thank “the man who has done more than perhaps anyone else to bring about this real revolution”—the Secretary of Health and Human Services, Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.

Trump’s executive order, which was not supported by any major independent medical organization, is perhaps the Administration’s most forthright attempt yet to upend federal vaccine recommendations. It has been touted as a major victory for R.F.K., Jr., whose time as Health Secretary has dismayed the public-health community. Under Kennedy, vaccine skeptics have been elevated to prominent positions and public-health agencies have suppressed the publication of scientific reports that diverge from his preferred narrative. (Officials have said that the reports were pulled owing to methodological concerns.) Parents are increasingly asking pediatricians to delay, space out, or altogether forgo immunizations for their children. State lawmakers have introduced hundreds of bills to weaken immunization rules and access, or to undermine trust in vaccines. There’s been a sharp uptick in the number of kindergarteners deemed exempt from such mandates; in some states, more than one in every eight remains unvaccinated against a preventable disease. Under the second Trump Administration, the United States has recorded more measles cases than it did in the preceding twenty-eight years.

It’s reasonable to worry that the R.F.K., Jr., era has set American science and medicine back in ways that might not be corrected for years, if ever. Yet it’s also possible to read Kennedy’s efforts, especially the new vaccine recommendations, less as triumphs than as flailing attempts to enact an unwelcome vision. Kennedy and his agenda are hardly popular. Public trust in the agencies he leads has fallen. The latest order, like prior attempts to undermine established vaccine guidance, will surely face legal challenges that limit its scope and impact.

Kennedy has argued that “there is no vaccine that is, you know, safe and effective,” and that the COVID shot was the “deadliest vaccine ever made.” But, as the nation’s top health official, he has struggled to actualize his maximalist rhetoric in the way that other Administration officials have theirs. Trump’s Department of Homeland Security says that it deported more than half a million people in the President’s first year back in office, sending some to countries they’ve never been to. The Department of Justice has launched pretextual prosecutions against the President’s political opponents. Elon Musk bragged about throwing U.S.A.I.D., an agency estimated to have saved millions of lives around the world, into a “wood chipper.” In the meantime, measles immunization rates among kindergarteners have fallen by less than one per cent. The share of kindergarteners with formal exemptions from vaccine mandates rose from 3.6 per cent to 4.2 per cent. These are troubling developments, to be sure, and enough to contribute to an unprecedented rise in infections. But, for now, we are not living in the worst-case scenarios that some envisioned when Kennedy took office. A year and a half into his tenure, is R.F.K., Jr., winning or losing?

A century ago, the Italian Marxist philosopher Antonio Gramsci was arrested and imprisoned for his opposition to Mussolini’s Fascist regime. In his “Prison Notebooks,” Gramsci continued to advocate for social change, but, fearing censorship, developed a metaphor based on the trench warfare of the First World War. Society, he argued, could be transformed through a “war of maneuver” or a “war of position.” A war of maneuver refers to the abrupt seizure of political control, such as Germany’s invasion of Belgium or the Bolshevik overthrow of the tsarist government in Russia. A war of position, in contrast, proceeds slowly, wielding what Gramsci called “cultural hegemony” to shape how people see the world. Wars of maneuver win territory; wars of position win hearts and minds.

In the American context, the civil-rights movement was arguably a war of position, and so was the fight for marriage equality. Both culminated in victorious maneuvers—transformative legislation, Supreme Court decisions that expanded rights—but they were preceded by decades of cultural change. In Gramsci’s telling, wars of maneuver could succeed where the state had a tight grip and the institutions of civil society (churches, schools, unions, professional organizations, the press) were weak and malleable, as in Imperial Russia. But in Western nations he perceived a more equal balance between the state and civil-society institutions. The government was “only an outer ditch,” Gramsci wrote, “behind which there stood a powerful system of fortresses and earthworks.” This meant that winning a war of maneuver, whether in a coup or in a transformative election, might not be enough to effect lasting change. Indeed, Italian Fascism toppled at the end of the Second World War.

Before R.F.K., Jr., became Health Secretary, he argued that “the people who run our vaccine programs should be in jail” and compared their work to that of Nazi death camps. He accused them of covering up mass harm to children, arguing that “the pedophilia scandal in the Catholic Church is a perfect metaphor.” He suggested that after some children are immunized, “three months later their brain is gone,” and that doctors giving vaccines have “butchered” children and “poisoned an entire generation.” He said that he would “do anything” to go back in time and not immunize his own children. When he became Health Secretary, he was determined to change the system that he had long criticized. He reportedly wanted to abolish the childhood-vaccine schedule and dedicate more than a tenth of the N.I.H. budget to studying supposed links between vaccines and autism. (An H.H.S. spokesperson contacted by Reuters disputed that Kennedy wanted to abolish the schedule; the N.I.H. proposal was eventually dropped.)

Kennedy certainly made news for his maneuvers. He eliminated a quarter of the H.H.S. workforce at the direction of DOGE, removed the heads of research institutes, dismantled programs that protect against environmental toxins and infectious diseases, and replaced the members of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, a key C.D.C. vaccine-advisory group, with handpicked selections. But the net result was chaos, not coherent change. Kennedy’s mass layoffs, for instance, were carried out in such a haphazard fashion that he later described roughly twenty per cent of them as possible errors. He hadn’t meant to terminate a C.D.C. program dedicated to preventing lead poisoning in children, for example. “Personnel that should not have been cut were cut,” Kennedy said. Some of the fired employees have since been asked to return.

For all the damage that Kennedy has inflicted, his actions on vaccines have largely been piecemeal and procedural. He attempted to delay some infants’ first hepatitis-B vaccine dose by at least a few months, a move that could needlessly expose thousands of newborns to the virus, but was temporarily blocked by a federal judge on the ground that the illegally constituted ACIP had recommended the change. Without consulting C.D.C. scientists, Kennedy announced, on X, that healthy children and pregnant women no longer need the COVID vaccine—but, even before the announcement, less than fifteen per cent of children and pregnant women were getting the shot. “I’m actually somewhat surprised that he hasn’t totally gotten rid of COVID vaccines,” David Gorski, a surgeon at Wayne State University who manages the blog Science-Based Medicine, told me. “I think he’s probably just discovering that the bureaucracy is more difficult to move than he thought.”

Kennedy has arguably been constrained, not unleashed, under Trump. “Even a lot of Republicans don’t want to go where Kennedy wants to go,” Dorit Reiss, a vaccine-policy scholar at U.C. Law San Francisco, told me. White House advisers have argued that his vision would be politically injurious ahead of the midterms. Around the time that a prominent Republican pollster circulated a memo saying that “vaccine skepticism is bad politics,” one official said that the Administration was “done” with the issue. G.O.P. lawmakers also know that most of their constituents want to maintain access to vaccines. And so, for the most part, the Administration has not withdrawn its support for specific vaccines, a move that could spur insurance companies and public vaccination programs to stop covering them. Instead, it has issued far more muted advice, such as “shared clinical decision-making” between doctors and patients. After Kennedy swapped in his own people on the C.D.C.’s vaccine-advisory committee, Fiona Havers, an infectious-disease specialist and a former C.D.C. official, had a “huge fear” that children would lose access to immunizations, she told me. “But I think the Administration quickly realized that denying insurance coverage for vaccines was not a headline that played well.”

Even the recent effort to replace the combined M.M.R. vaccine with separate shots for measles, mumps, and rubella may have little effect. Such a change would likely lower vaccine uptake by making it more difficult for children to get all the vaccinations they need. But, in practice, separate shots for measles, mumps, and rubella aren’t even available in the U.S. Manufacturers estimate that it could take them a decade to bring them to market. Reiss told me that she is deeply concerned about the damage Kennedy has done: “He’s smashed norms of good governance—he’s done things by fiat in a non-deliberative, non-transparent way.” At the same time, she said, “He hasn’t wrecked our vaccine infrastructure in ways that can’t be fixed if a science-based Administration comes into power.” If the culmination of Kennedy’s crusade against vaccines is a set of narrow, legally contested, and reversible recommendations—recommendations plainly rejected by most medical professionals—then it is hard to argue that his war of maneuver has gained that much ground.

Of course, Trump and Kennedy are engaged in a war of position, too: they are working to change minds as well as policy. Trump won the election in 2024 by a greater margin than he had in 2016, and Kennedy has made meaningful strides toward normalizing his vaccine-skeptical views. Children’s Health Defense, an advocacy group that Kennedy helped bring to prominence, has become a leading purveyor of pseudoscience; a 2019 study found that, along with one other group, the organization had purchased more anti-vaccine Facebook advertisements than any other. Kennedy himself ranks among the “Disinformation Dozen,” as the Center for Countering Digital Hate labelled the twelve individuals who spread a large proportion of misleading medical information during the pandemic. Worryingly, the share of Americans who say that it’s very or extremely important that parents get their children vaccinated has fallen sharply in recent decades. Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement, which got its name just two years ago, now counts more than forty per cent of the country as supporters.

There’s reason to think that even these gains are less dramatic than they appear, though. Support for MAHA depends heavily on MAGA, the Trumpian movement after which it was named. And the most important issue to MAHA voters is not the abolition of vaccines but the affordability of health care. According to the health-news site KFF, only a tenth of the movement’s supporters cite vaccines as their top priority, and nearly eighty per cent of parents in the movement believe that the M.M.R. shot is safe. After South Carolina experienced a major measles outbreak last year, vaccination surged; in one hard-hit area, nearly twice as many M.M.R. doses were administered in early 2026 than had been in the same period of the previous year. Today, the vast majority of Americans still say that they trust doctors and scientists for information about their health. Faith in Kennedy started low and has fallen further. Just after he took office, almost half of Americans disapproved of him; in an April poll, sixty per cent of voters did.

“Things could be worse” is no cause for celebration. Rather, it should be a call to action. Gramsci argued that the period between an old order and a new one was a “time of monsters,” when extreme movements and dangerous leaders reared their heads. Confronting them required a “pessimism of the intellect”—a readiness to take the peril seriously—in addition to an “optimism of the will.” The battle for sound vaccine policy and effective public health is worth fighting, and it is winnable. Earlier this year, the American Academy of Pediatrics and other groups prevailed in a lawsuit against Kennedy’s reconstitution of the C.D.C.’s vaccine-advisory committee, stalling its overhaul of the childhood-vaccine schedule (the government has appealed). State governments have banded together to develop their own vaccine guidance, rejecting the recommendations of an increasingly unreliable federal government. The nation’s largest association of health insurers has committed to continue covering, at no cost to patients, all ACIP-recommended immunizations, at least through the end of next year. It can be easy to feel hopeless in the face of a senseless assault on science. But it is not too late to shore up the fortresses and earthworks. Many still appear to be holding—for now. ♦

Dhruv Khullar, a contributing writer at The New Yorker, is a practicing physician and an associate professor at Weill Cornell Medical College. He writes about medicine, health care, and politics.

title: Dolphins and Other Lovers
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
As Eliran Arazi spends time with the Andoque, an Indigenous people in southern Colombia along the Caquetá River, he finds himself increasingly drawn into their tales that interweave sexuality with the creatures of the jungle. Gradually, those stories begin to shape his own way of thinking about seduction in modern life, as his mind spins off its own fantasies. A fascinating piece that blurs the lines between writer and subject, leaving the reader in a dreamlike state.

A few days later, jaguar footprints appeared along the long path leading to a small harbour on the Caquetá River. For the next week, Dufi’s family expressed concerns about venturing down that path, especially alone, for fear of a jaguar attack. When I mentioned my plan to go there for a phone call, hoping for better reception by the river, one of Dufi’s sons again cautioned me about the jaguar. Dufi, however, quickly reassured me. I had nothing to fear because jaguars dislike the soapy, perfumed scent of white people, which, he added, is precisely the smell that attracts dolphins.

As I reached the Caquetá in the late afternoon, I sensed the dolphin smell again. Odours and attraction, I thought – at least it works both ways.

More picks on anthropology

title: The Sound of Your Voice
author: Krista Stevens
content:
What defines success when it comes to music? For Hrishikesh Hirway, who wrote four albums under the name The One AM Radio, it meant commercial attention. His interest in making music cooled after sales and airplay failed to materialize; he went 15 years without releasing an album. In this essay for The Bitter Southerner, Hirway looks at how he overcame perfectionism to write and record In the Last Hour of Light, an album heavy on collaboration.

“But Phil was echoing something I’d heard in the interviews I’d conducted and read about in books on writing: separate your creative, generative side from your editing, critical side. They push in opposite directions, and as soon as you start to edit, you’re no longer as free to play.”

“It was two days after my 47th birthday, which had left me feeling melancholy about reaching middle age and still feeling so far from my goals. I sat on my couch, put my headphones on, and played the album. Something had shifted for me. Somewhere around the third song, I felt something for the first time: I loved what I was hearing.

The music brought back memories with perfect clarity: what it felt like to write each song, to record them, the long journey to transform a part of myself into this music. It was no longer a question of the music’s worth. I can say to myself: this album is a document. And in it —listen!—you’re alive.”

More picks from The Bitter Southerner

“With little fanfare, Ray Di Pietro has attracted tens of thousands of devotees. His images are artfully composed, spontaneous, honest, and, well, kind.”

My 24 Guitars

Elissa Altman | The Bitter Southerner | August 19, 2025 | 4,204 words

“Music was hazardous in my family, yet I couldn’t help playing—even in my sleep.”

Woman in the Woods

Holly Haworth | The Bitter Southerner | September 8, 2024 | 2,884 words

“To me, the woods are an intricate tapestry in which I always try to see the bigger picture.”

title: My pilgrimage to Mecca in the age of the golf-cart and mall | Aeon Essays
content:
It is Ramadan, the holiest month of the Islamic calendar, and I am sitting in a rooftop café in Mecca, the holiest city of the religion. The sun has gone down, and an array of glittering shops and hotels lights up the urban expanse below me. At the heart of this ancient city, the foremost site of Muslim worship, guarded with fortress-like marble walls, is the Masjid al-haram complex – the largest mosque in the world. I’ve just completed my own pilgrimage to the holy site, and I’m struggling to name the discomfort that I am feeling.

There are few words to describe the whiplash of coming face to face with a Joe & The Juice, a Sephora and a plethora of other shops and hotels and Times Square-style billboards after going through one of the most spiritually charged experiences of my life. To find myself in what seemed just like any other petrodollar-fuelled Gulf port instead of a sanctified land was jarring. I felt robbed of the romanticism I had expected after a childhood built on admiration for religious lore and high-flown notions of a fantastical divine city.

I’d found myself in Mecca, trying to catch a break from the existential dread of my day-to-day life – the constant round of applying for jobs I didn’t really want because it wasn’t sustainable to write full-time, going on first date after first date, trying to find love on apps that were designed for failure, doomscrolling social media while caught in a dopamine trap, and staring at my laptop screen while waiting for some revelation to break through the fog in my mind and string itself into life-changing words. My 30s were closing in, and I felt the noose of squandered potential around my neck.

One of my most frequent prayers comes from a verse in the Quran that narrates Moses’ escape from Egypt: ‘Rabbi inni lima anzalta ilayya min khairin faqir’ (‘My Lord, indeed I am in absolute need of whatever good You send down’). I have always been comforted by the notion that a divine power was looking after me, that something out there existed beyond the constraints of time and space – omnipresent, omnipotent – and yet closer to me than my jugular vein, as my Holy Book would tell me.

My rationale for the trip was that this kind of spiritual sugar rush would allow me to find my footing in the secular world. My worshipful hope was that God would be impressed by my performed devotion, and divine intervention would set my worldly affairs straight. And though I felt a sense of renewed worship in making my pilgrimage, that break from the ordinary world never came.

Islam is not an ascetic faith: interestingly, it prohibits monasticism. However, the state of being a pilgrim is the closest that one comes to forsaking the material world. Before entering the boundaries of the Holy City, dressed in a swishing white abaya with a prayer book hung on a lanyard around my neck, I had committed to a state of heightened spiritual purity known as the ihram.

The word ihram has etymological roots in the word haraam, which means to forbid. It is the embodiment of additional, out-of-the-ordinary prohibitions. In this consecrated state, pilgrims are not allowed to have sexual relations or to hunt an animal or to change the state of their body: they cannot cut their nails or hair, for example, or perfume themselves. Men must cover themselves only with two pieces of unstitched cloth, while women must wear unadorned garments that leave their faces and hands visible. The purpose of the ihram is to equalise worshippers for the duration of their pilgrimage. As the anthropologists Victor Turner and Edith Turner described (albeit in the context of Christianity), pilgrims occupy a liminal, threshold state. They enter a state of structural betweenness, termed ‘communitas’, where they find themselves stripped of their social identities, and in a temporary state of spontaneous egalitarianism.

There are two kinds of pilgrimages in the faith, the umrah – which takes a few hours to complete and can be done at any time of the year, and the Hajj – which takes five days, and can be performed only in the Islamic month of Dhul-Hijjah. Both pilgrimages require the same conditions of ihram. I began my umrah with a short ride to the Mosque on a government-funded shuttle service, decorated with an electric ticker that said: ‘Welcome Guests of Ar Rahman’, that is, guests of the Most Merciful. Pilgrims are not guests of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, but of God, and therefore, on paper, both prince and pauper must be alike. When in communitas, this sentiment feels enacted.

It is hard to look away from the symbol of your faith made manifest before you

Some pilgrims prayed on the shuttle with prayer beads, others read out verses from the Quran apps on their phones. Others still had prayer books similar to mine. But as we got closer to the Great Mosque, we were let off the bus, and everyone’s rhythmic chanting came into unison in a single phrase, as pilgrims cried out to the skies ‘Labbaik Allahumma Labbaik’ (‘Oh, here I am, my Lord! I have answered your call!’) The fervent declaration continued as we joined the crowd of thousands making their way on foot into the heart of Masjid al-Haram.

The first thing you experience when you enter the Great Mosque of Mecca is the smell of oudh and rosewater engulfing you. A cultural belief among many Muslim communities is that whatever you pray for when you first glance upon the Kaaba – the black raw-silk-covered cuboid stone at the centre of the mosque – will be granted, so most pilgrims enter for the first time with their eyes firmly planted on the cool marble floor – or held tightly shut as they hold on to the person guiding them in. And when you do open your eyes, that initial glance is surreal; an ocean of pilgrims clad in white circumambulate the Kaaba, flocks of swallows flit against the skyline, and there are hundreds of things in the periphery of your sightlines to be distracted by – from the towering malls to surveillance drones and battalions of guards with puffed chests patrolling against miscreants. Yet, despite these competing spectacles, it is hard to look away from the symbol of your faith made manifest before you – more enormous than you imagined, impossibly still, magnetic.

The Kaaba is an epitomic example of what Mircea Eliade, a foundational historian of religions, described in The Sacred and the Profane (1957) as ‘axis mundi’, or the navel of the Earth, a centre from which the world is said to have emerged. In Islamic belief, Mecca is the mother city, the land from which the rest of the world rolled out. In the same theology, the Kaaba was the first building on Earth, established for the worship of God, before being lost in the flood of Noah and then rebuilt by Abraham and his son Ismael in its present form.

Since Muhammad’s conquest of Mecca in 630 CE, the Kaaba has oriented all aspects of Muslim life. Wherever they are in the world, Muslims perform their five daily prayers facing towards the Kaaba, and dead bodies are buried with their head oriented in the same direction. The complex built around it encompasses all of the sacred topography you must go through on your pilgrimage. You start with the circumambulation of the Kaaba, before praying adjacent to the Maqam-e-Ibrahim, a stone enclosed in glass, which is supposed to bear the footprints of Abraham. Then, you must cross the distance between the hills of Safa and Marwa seven times, a total of 3.15 km (1.96 miles). Once these obligatory rituals of the umrah (which take a few hours) have been completed, men shave their heads, while women cut an inch or two of their hair to exit the state of being a pilgrim.

For Eliade, the sacred space marks a break from the locus of mundane, profane life. It is an anchor emerging through divine revelation, from which believers orient themselves, allowing access to a more primordial state of being. In the state of ihraam – eyes upon the anchor that had shaped my worship – my experience was more metaphysical than embodied. In those moments, I occupied an imagined Mecca, the fabled city of prophets and angels, and of mothers striving to keep faith in the face of cruel oppression. I could almost see what had been here before, the ghosts of a nascent faith, taking its first shaky breaths, keeping step with the flesh-and-bone believers centuries away.

Accessing that spiritual world required me to suspend my disbelief – because, in 2026, even the Great Mosque is, like Mecca itself, very different from the one I had read about in prophetic traditions. In the past decade, the mosque has been subject to a massive expansion and renovation project. At a cost of nearly $26.6 billion, the Saudi government has rebuilt the complex, growing it from 414,000 square metres to 1.564 million square metres of space, in order to accommodate a growing number of pilgrims and to make the area more accessible. However, this has come at a great cost to the historicity of the space and, to an extent, to the otherworldliness that the line between sacred and profane demands.

Except for the Kaaba, all historically significant structures in the complex have been either modified or destroyed

Four floors of marble walkways now surround the Kaaba, allowing more people to circumambulate at once. The different floors are accessed through a network of escalators and ramps. The final walkway comes with tracks for golf carts – and, at the price of 300 Saudi riyals ($80), pilgrims can complete their rituals on wheels. Those on a budget, meanwhile, can spend half that amount to rent a wheelchair if they’re struggling with walking more than the 2.5 miles expected.

In her travelogue Pilgrimage to Mecca (1934), Lady Evelyn Cobbold, the first British female convert to make the Hajj, wrote:

Even the Ford Motor could not vulgarise the lovely moon-splashed desert, whose stillness was unbroken by a camel caravan we passed, silently treading its way Northward; mysterious phantoms of beasts and men of another world than ours – I inwardly prayed that the motor may never displace the camel.

I wonder what she would make of the carts zipping through the mosque itself today. The consequence of these efficiency-oriented measures is that, except for the Kaaba, all historically significant structures in the Mecca complex have been either modified or destroyed.

The path between the hills of Safa and Marwa, where Muslims believe that the Prophet’s wife Hagar foraged for water, before the spring of holy water, Zamzam, miraculously burst open, has now been flattened and reconstructed as a multistorey, air-conditioned enclosure. The structure that marked the well of holy water has also been demolished, with pilgrims now able to access the water only through taps and tanks. Canopies dedicated to influential classical scholars of Islam within the mosque complex have been dismantled, while neon lights have been installed to mark the point at which circumambulation is to begin.

As I went through the rituals, the chasm between the sacred space in my mind and the very real, remade-for-modern-convenience one I occupied provoked a kind of grief. I mourned that these weren’t the same floors the forebears of my faith had walked, nor were these the pillars they had leaned against. On one hand, that sense of communitas with the other pilgrims nourished my soul; on the other, I was palpably aware of how much of a disjuncture I was at with the past. When I completed my pilgrimage, I reached under the swathes of my hijab to snip off a few curls from my head with small metal scissors. Exiting the state of ihram and physically changed by my acts of worship, I was pushed into a painful awareness of the mundane, profane world. The disjuncture became significantly more pronounced when I stepped out of the mosque.

In Cobbold’s memoir, written less than a century ago, Mecca is the city without walls, protected by mountains, with Bedouin caravans selling wares to pilgrims staying in modest homestays and camping on the desert trail. That Mecca no longer exists either. The homestays are gone, and the hospitable locals of yore now live on the outskirts of the city – their neighbourhoods swallowed up by hotels and shopping complexes.

Some changes are unavoidable. When Muhammad performed his final pilgrimage in 632 CE, an estimated 30,000 followers accompanied him. When I performed my pilgrimage in February 2026, an estimated 1.68 million people from abroad had been granted pilgrimage permits for the month of Ramadan. These pilgrims need space not just to worship, but also to sleep and eat, and to do all that mortal bodies do – and so infrastructure should be built to support those needs.

However, the de-historicisation of Mecca has been a calculated, ideological project, with what would be considered protected monuments in any other part of the world decimated to build vanity projects. Saudi Arabia’s premier religious ideology – Wahhabism – is an 18th-century revivalist movement that espouses a literalist, strict interpretation of the Quran, and it has encouraged the tearing down of historical sites such as the houses of early Islamic figures, and the enshrined gravesites of the Prophet’s family, claiming that they’d invite idolatry otherwise. The refitting of Mecca is also deeply entwined with the rise of the petrodollar in the Kingdom, creating a tense intersection where ritual jostles with capitalism for space. As the writer and public intellectual Ziauddin Sardar puts it in The Sacred City (2014), the Kingdom has made a steel and glass heaven of consumerism in the name of extinguishing idol worship.

Where those before us battled drought and death to find God, we battle excess and the temptation of abundance

So, now, a Hilton Hotel stands where the house of Islam’s first Caliph, Abu Bakr, once stood. A nondescript library stands in place of the home in which Muhammad was born, while an 18th-century citadel was torn down to make way for the Makkah Clock Tower complex, a collection of seven buildings that are part mall, part hotel. The tallest of these buildings is a Big Ben-esque structure, sporting a giant clock dial that overlooks the Kaaba.

On the back of the oil economy, the Kingdom has exported its brand of Wahhabi Islam across the world. Traditional ways of believing have been homogenised, and a dogmatic, cookie-cutter version of the faith has been parcelled off. In return, the Global North has exported the phenomenon of placelessness to Saudi Arabia, whereby an influx of foreign brands has remade both the country’s high streets and consumer choices. The commercial onslaught, compounded by the active destruction of material history, gives the fringes of sacred space a particular tone. Irfan al-Alawi, a theologian and heritage preservation proponent, described this in The Guardian as the ‘Manhattanisation of Mecca’.

As I walked through the grey concrete streets and glass malls of Mecca, I wondered if devotion here would have meant more when the skyline was dotted with sandy hills, and there was nothing but the House of God as your harbour against the angry desert. I contemplated whether my return to a comfortable hotel bed, and not a flimsy tent, implied something lacking in my commitment to giving up the material. Or perhaps it is just that I am of this time, and my prayers are subject to its whims. Indeed, perhaps it is in that very unease that ritual finds meaning – if all the world were holy, we would not gravitate as we do to the omphalos (literally, ‘navel’). The sacred is significant because it disrupts the profane. Where those before us battled drought and death to find God, we must battle excess and the temptation of abundance.

I can’t presume to know what God thinks of today’s Mecca. After all, to evolve is natural to the holy city; it has been moulded to dynasties and clerical moods over centuries. Belief continues to move past anachronisms, and yet, as one prays by the black-and-gold cloth-covered Kaaba, the shadow of the clock towers falls upon you – a too-obvious metaphor in action.

title: Volcanoes That Made History - Nautilus
content:
This story was originally published by Knowable Magazine.

Featured Video

The first telegram arrived in Singapore on a Monday, sent from the city of Batavia in the Dutch East Indies (now Jakarta, Indonesia). “Terrific detonations from Krakatau (volcanic island),” it reported. Soon afterward: “Stones falling. Village near Anjer washed away.” The wires continued clattering out news of bridges destroyed, boats smashed, lighthouses “disappeared.” By noon on Tuesday, the scope of the natural disaster was clear: “Where once Mount Krakatau stood the sea now plays.”

Within days, the source of the destruction was known worldwide. On the morning of August 27, 1883, a volcanic eruption had obliterated two islands in the strait between Java and Sumatra, and most of a third. More than 36,000 people perished, the majority in devastating tsunamis that raced outward from the colossal explosion.

Thanks to Victorian-era telecommunications, it was the first time in history that people around the globe could begin to document, in near real time, the immediate and long-term effects of a catastrophic volcanic eruption. What they learned over the next few years laid the foundations for the modern science of volcanology. And it was an especially eye-opening lesson in how the biggest eruptions can influence climate, agriculture and even the course of human history.

Global Effects

In the months after Krakatau, drifting volcanic particles high in the atmosphere circled the globe, causing violently colored sunsets that contemporary artists captured in paintings, likely including the psychedelic background of Edvard Munch’s The Scream.

But the key climate-driving component of the volcano’s emissions was sulfur from the molten rock that fed Krakatau. Once sulfur erupts into the atmosphere, it can form particles called aerosols that reflect sunlight and cool Earth. In the months and years after the eruption, average summer temperatures fell 0.6 degrees Celsius (1.1 degrees Fahrenheit) in the non-tropical regions of the Northern Hemisphere.

Fast-forward more than a century, and researchers now understand that climate changes, especially rapid ones, have transformed societies by affecting agriculture, public health and living conditions. With what they’ve learned from Krakatau and other eruptions, volcanologists today are identifying past catastrophic blasts that may have contributed to historic events like droughts, famines, epidemics and societal unrest.

“In so many different ways societies were affected … a failure in harvest or flooding or a cold summer or a really cold winter,” says Katrin Kleemann, an environmental historian at the German Maritime Museum in Bremerhaven.

While they can’t prove an eruption caused the demise of a regime, volcanologists have uncovered some intriguing links, including some that could inform our understanding of how today’s society might react to a rapidly changing climate.

536 and All That

The first challenge in making volcano-society connections is to find physical fingerprints of past eruptions. In the year 536, scribes in Europe, the Middle East and Asia wrote about bizarre weather, including a haze that shrouded the sun for 18 months. Temperatures plummeted, harvests failed, and within a few years the first documented global plague began.

These early medieval chronicles strongly suggest a major volcanic eruption—but the hard evidence lies deep in polar ice. Scientists can infer that big eruptions happened at certain times in the past by looking for sulfur and ash deposits in ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica. These cores, drilled into ice sheets, preserve an annual record of whatever was circulating in Earth’s atmosphere as it settled onto the surface each year. Researchers can read these frozen layers back in time like turning the pages of a book.

It turns out that polar ice cores do contain large amounts of sulfur dating to 536, a distinct signal of a major eruption. But which volcano went off at the time remains a mystery. There is no known written record from anyone living close to the eruption—Iceland, where it may have occurred, was not yet populated.

Empire Falls

There is better evidence pinpointing the volcano that may have helped topple the Mongol Empire seven centuries later. Until 2013, researchers knew only that some eruption—the biggest in the last few millennia as measured by sulfur output—occurred in 1257. In 2013, an interdisciplinary team radiocarbon-dated the ash, pumice and other deposits around Samalas, a volcano in Indonesia, tying it to the 1257 eruption.

Tree-ring studies, which analyze annual growth layers on trees to determine which years had good and bad growing weather, show extensive cooling across North America and Eurasia from 1257 to 1259. Among other impacts, bad harvests led to starvation in England, and wet, cool summer weather in Japan damaged rice production.

Some researchers have speculated that it was the Samalas eruption that helped seal the fate of the Mongol Empire, which ended after its last ruler perished in a 1259 epidemic in China that could have been linked with the eruption-caused climate changes.

The Black Death

A century after Samalas, volcanologists have found, there was yet another intriguing eruption-disease connection. Between 1346 and 1352, perhaps half of Europe’s population died in the Black Death plague, from infection by the flea-borne bacterium Yersinia pestis.

Historical records from Europe and Asia suggest that skies were darker than usual around that time, perhaps because of a volcanic haze. Ice-core records support that interpretation, documenting a big eruption, or perhaps several, around the year 1345 — though the location remains unknown.

To see how this volcanic activity might have affected climate, an interdisciplinary team led by Ulf Büntgen, a tree-ring specialist at the University of Cambridge, used tree-ring data to confirm that the summers of 1345, 1346 and 1347 were unusually cold and wet in southern Europe.

Büntgen and his colleagues note that as crops failed in the bad weather, Europeans imported grain from farther east. The grain ships arrived with rats harboring Y. pestis, leading the researchers to argue that the mystery volcano erupting in 1345 may have set off a chain of events that ultimately killed tens of millions of people.

Iceland’s Toxic Frogs

Connecting volcanoes to human events may be a challenge even today, but in 1784 an American ambassador to France named Benjamin Franklin was astute enough to link a strange haze that rolled across the countryside in the previous year to a distant eruption.

The source turns out to be Laki, an Icelandic fissure that spewed lava for eight months starting in June 1783. The eruption killed at least one-fifth of Iceland’s people, and much of its livestock, through toxic fog and climate changes that ruined harvests. Though the event was well-documented in Iceland, observers in England, France and elsewhere across Europe who saw the volcano’s haze and sometimes smelled its foul odor could only guess what was going on in a disconnected, pre-electronic world.

“They wouldn’t get news alerts on their phone, they wouldn’t see livestreams of this eruption — they would have no idea,” says Kleemann, who has studied the eruption.

Connections Grow Clearer

Though it happened just a few decades after Laki, one of the largest eruptions in recorded human history offers a much more detailed picture of how a volcanic climate shock can change history. In 1815, a mountain in Indonesia named Tambora exploded, sending sulfur into the upper atmosphere and triggering broad climatic changes.

Tambora’s eruption caused cooling across much of Europe and North America, where crops failed and 1816 was dubbed the “year without a summer.” The volcanic weather that year kept the writer Mary Shelley cooped up while traveling in Switzerland, where she wrote the novel Frankenstein.

The bad weather brought famine to Switzerland, Ireland and elsewhere; grain prices and malnutrition soared in parts of Europe, prompting tens of thousands of people to emigrate to North America. Eastern Europe and western Russia, in contrast, had relatively better growing conditions under the post-volcanic climate and enough grain to export it to other nations. Port cities like London and Hamburg enjoyed greater access to imported grains, while prices rose sharply in the hinterlands. Those bright spots show how access to transportation and trade networks can make societies more resilient in the face of disaster.

“Human society has a lot of susceptibilities and vulnerabilities,” says Clive Oppenheimer, a volcanologist at the University of Cambridge who coauthored a 2026 Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences paper on volcanoes, climate and society with Büntgen. “Some climate shocks will come and go…. At other times, the climate shock will come ... when there are greater societal vulnerabilities.”

These lessons may hold particular relevance today, because researchers see the historical fallout of past eruptions as a clue to how humanity might respond to present-day climate change. Big volcanic eruptions cool the planet rather than warm it, but they represent the same sort of rapid planetwide shocks that societies are coping with now as Earth heats up.

And as historical volcanology teaches, it is only a matter of time before the next big blast. In the era of satellites and social media saturation, the whole world will know the moment it happens — but it is only by studying past events like Krakatau and Tambora that we can have an idea of what will happen next.

This article originally appeared in Knowable Magazine, a nonprofit publication dedicated to making scientific knowledge accessible to all. Sign up for Knowable Magazine’s newsletter.

title: The Fantasy Behind Trump’s Anti-Smithsonian Crusade
author: @NewYorker
content:
Trump claims that the institution has fallen into the hands of Marxist radicals. A stroll through the exhibitions suggests otherwise.

August 20, 2026

The Immokalee Statue of Liberty in “Many Voices, One Nation,” at the National Museum of American History.Photograph by Lawren Simmons

Earlier this month, when I visited the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History (N.M.A.H.), President Trump’s signage warning of its “ideological capture” had yet to be installed. National Guardsmen marched in the paralyzing heat, which, along with the shadows cast by a revolving sculpture in the courtyard, suggested the eerie calm before the gunfight in a Western. Finally, the silence was broken by laughter—a group of volunteers from Citizen Historians for the Smithsonian, who’d advised me, via text, to look out for “4 old white ladies 🧓🏼🧑🏼‍🦳🧓🏼🧑🏼‍🦳”

“I just think what’s going on is a false narrative,” Deborah Greenbush, a D.C. tour guide who’s taken countless visitors through the museum, said. “I have never once had any adult or youngster express the feeling that what they saw made them feel bad. If it’s factual and actual, we should talk about it.” Next to her were Cindy Stevens, a former public-housing administrator, and Pege Gilgannon, a former photojournalist, who wore a shirt emblazoned with the words “Free D.C.” (She frequently volunteers for the D.C.-statehood movement.) Leading the group was Patti Curtis, a STEM adviser at the Department of Education, who retired just before its DOGE-driven evisceration. “They eliminated the entire research department,” she said. “I’m grateful that the Smithsonian isn’t just rolling over like some of our federal agencies.”

The four women are neighbors, and belong to a nonprofit community for seniors. “It’s your second family,” Gilgannon explained. “So you don’t just sit there playing mah-jongg.” Last summer, Curtis persuaded them to join Citizen Historians, a grassroots effort to monitor Smithsonian exhibitions for political interference. She’d heard about the group from one of its founders, James Millward, a central-Asia scholar at Georgetown. “He said, ‘I’ve taught in China and seen history erased, and I don’t want it to happen here.’ ” Not long before, Trump had pressured the director of the National Portrait Gallery, Kim Sajet, to resign, in part because his official portrait’s wall text mentioned his two impeachments. Curtis organized forty volunteers to photograph its collections; altogether, more than seven hundred people have participated in Citizen Historian campaigns.

Trump’s anti-Smithsonian crusade began in March, 2025, with an executive order called “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History.” A declaration of war against a “revisionist movement” that saw America as “irredeemably flawed,” the order called for the removal of “improper ideology” from the Smithsonian’s twenty-one museums, and threatened to slash the institution’s funding if it didn’t comply. Soon, there were panicked reports—later debunked—that artifacts from slavery and the civil-rights movement had been quietly removed.

For a year, though, the Smithsonian has been spared, in part because of its semi-independent status. It’s governed by a seventeen-member Board of Regents, which includes the Vice-President, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, six federal lawmakers, and nine congressionally appointed members of the general public. The institution’s secretary, Lonnie G. Bunch III, has defended its integrity, but also shrewdly avoided provocative shows of resistance. Last August, he reportedly charmed Trump over lunch at the White House, and by the start of this summer’s Semiquincentennial celebrations, it was almost possible to believe that the Administration had moved on. Then, on July 4th, the White House Domestic Policy Council published a report called “Saving America’s Story,” which alleges that the N.M.A.H. has been hijacked by a cohort of radical activists. Shortly thereafter, Trump ordered the National Park Service to install warning signs outside the museum, whose director, Anthea Hartig, was summoned to testify on Capitol Hill.

“I was disturbed to hear about the quetzal,” Morgan Griffith, a congressman from Virginia, told Hartig, alluding to the suspiciously foreign bird feathers in a children’s show about money. (Quetzal feathers were once used as currency by the Aztecs and their trading partners in the American Southwest.) Nancy Mace, of South Carolina, called Hartig an ally of “queer pedophiles,” adducing, as evidence, a photo of RuPaul from an exhibition on American pop culture. Republicans also played a montage of Hartig making land acknowledgments, demanded to know why she’d once said that “loving America is very complicated,” and expressed outrage that no special exhibitions had been mounted about the Founding Fathers or the Declaration of Independence.

Democrats denounced the proceedings as a totalitarian show trial. Their star witness, the Pulitzer-winning historian David W. Blight, called the White House report “a declaration of political war on the historian’s profession,” and scoffed at accusations of left-wing revisionism. “All history is revision,” he said. “Would you prefer your doctors not to be revisionists?” Hartig, by contrast, was polite almost to the point of meekness, constrained by her role to “Sir”ing and “Ma’am”ing her inquisitors while affirming her commitment to a patriotism that was “not instructed but inspired.” She invited lawmakers to “walk the building with me” and “stand in front of the Star-Spangled Banner, in awe”—implying, not without reason, that many had never even visited the museum they were so determined to control.

If they did come, the Citizen Historians were determined to get there first. Curtis unfolded a map of the museum with eight galleries circled in hot pink. “We powwowed last night and realized we could hit four of them,” she explained. “Rather than split up, let’s go together and saturate.”

“Can anybody read that?” Gilgannon whispered, holding her phone up like a flashlight.

“Yeah, ‘Oh say can you see by the dawn’s early light,’ ” Curtis replied.

We were standing in the darkened chamber that houses the Star-Spangled Banner, whose tattered stripes were dimly visible behind glass. The flag was made by Mary Pickersgill, who sewed it with the help of her daughter, two nieces, and an “African-American indentured servant” named Grace Wisher. Curtis frowned. “Do we really think she was an ‘indentured servant’?” she asked, wondering if the label had originally read “slave.” Gilgannon sighed: “I hate how they put it in your head that you’re gonna get tricked.”

The White House report contends that N.M.A.H. has abandoned patriotism and erased the Founding Fathers in service of an “anti-white agenda” that seeks to “divide, dispirit, and discourage our citizens.” But a quick search of the collections database revealed that nearly a hundred objects associated with George Washington and the Revolutionary War—including Washington’s uniform, his battle sword, and his dinner plates—were on display. From the Star-Spangled Banner, we made our way to Horatio Greenough’s 1841 sculpture of a shirtless, sword-bearing Washington, its caption explaining how the sculptor had captured his “highest and noblest virtues.” Greenbush, the tour guide, was amused by his neoclassically bare chest. “He would have been mortified, I’m sure.”

Behind Washington was “Many Voices, One Nation,” an exhibition about the struggle of disparate peoples to forge an American identity. A video collage showcasing America’s diversity played on loop near the entrance; Gilgannon, whose family comes from Belgium, said, “My mother’s in there.” The four women fanned out to photograph the objects on display: an Irish brooch, a Chinese-American shop sign, a collection of accessories abandoned by migrants in the Sonoran Desert. The report frames the show as “pro-illegal alien activism,” but hadn’t mentioned its Border Patrol uniform, whose caption praised the agent’s twenty-two years of service. Later, we gawked at the lavishly decorated 1963 Chevy Impala in “Corazón y vida,” another exhibit derided as a paean to “foreign” peoples—the Chicanos of Southern California, who started building “lowriders” with elaborate hydraulic systems in the nineteen-forties. “I think I’d be scared when it lifts up,” Curtis said, inspecting the undercarriage. “We went to see ‘The Odyssey’ in 4DX a few weeks ago and I was screaming!”

On the top floor was “American Democracy,” a sweeping exhibition about self-governance. Near the entrance was the desk where Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence. Farther in was paraphernalia from a quarter millennium of Presidential campaigns, including Trump’s. (There was even a MAGA hat.) The exhibition culminated in a display of protest signs. The report characterizes them as “almost all for various progressive causes,” and I quickly spotted slogans familiar from Black Lives Matter and the campaign for marriage equality. But equally prominent were “Secure Our Borders,” “Stop Abortion Now,” and projected footage from a Tea Party rally—all unmentioned. Gilgannon took a picture of one from the D.C.-statehood movement. “They practice and promote joy,” she explained. “At first, I thought, What’s this crazy woo-woo? But that’s what’s going to bond us together when we have to, like, fight the National Guard.”

There was plenty of joy in “Entertainment Nation,” a bright, busy, and noisily media-rich survey of American pop culture. Greeting visitors was a photo of the jazz trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie, a “cool, Cold Warrior” who used music to fight Communism. Nearby was the sheet music for Irving Berlin’s “God Bless America” and Dorothy’s ruby slippers from “The Wizard of Oz,” whose L.G.B.T.Q. affiliations somehow escaped Republican scrutiny. It took several minutes for Greenbush and me to find the exhibition’s most controversial inclusion—an animation sketch depicting Mickey Mouse’s début in “Steamboat Willie” (1928), whose caption links the character to “longstanding traditions of blackface minstrelsy.” For once, a Citizen Historian and the report were on the same side. “Who would even make that connection?” Greenbush scoffed. “Maybe I’m naïve, but I never would have thought that. And there were points where I did watch a lot of Mickey Mouse.”

During the hearings, Representative Brandon Gill, of Texas, asked Hartig a question precision-engineered to extract a disqualifying sound bite: “Is Mickey Mouse racist?” When she said no, Gill quoted the caption—and again, Hartig affirmed Mickey’s innocence. “You don’t think blackface minstrelsy is racist?” Gill asked, now genuinely confused. Hartig kept calm. “It’s not for me to determine what’s problematic,” she replied. “It’s for me to determine what’s accurate.”

It’s well established that the Mickey Mouse of “Steamboat Willie”—who wears white gloves and performs the minstrel standard “Turkey in the Straw” on a paddle steamer—has its roots in blackface, which was, for nearly a century, one of America’s most popular forms of entertainment. To Republican lawmakers, pointing this out is character assassination, an attempt to cancel poor Mickey and all who hold him dear. But if Representative Gill visited the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American Culture, he might be surprised to learn how many great Black entertainers—including Eubie Blake and Josephine Baker—share Mickey’s checkered beginnings, and with what impartial curiosity these are explored.

Our tour of “Entertainment Nation” concluded with a video installation called “What’s So Funny?” It juxtaposed racist moments in old films and cartoons—Judy Garland dancing in blackface, Bugs Bunny fighting the Indian Wars—with excerpts from the routines of nonwhite comedians such as Margaret Cho and Richard Pryor. We laughed and cringed by turns, our faces painted by the light from the projectors. The 1946 film “Song of the South” came on, and I could feel us all torn between humming along to “Zip-A-Dee-Do-Dah”—a song that my grandmother, a Black woman, loves enough that she once bought an alarm clock with the melody—and recoiling in shame from Uncle Remus’s toothy grin. “My grandfather was actually in minstrel shows,” Greenbush abruptly volunteered. And yet, there she was, protecting our messy common heritage from being wiped clean.

How did the Smithsonian commemorate American history in simpler times, before postmodernism, intersectionality, and the many other Hydra heads of “woke”? The museum’s Semiquincentennial exhibitions struck me as neutral enough. But in order to assess their patriotism objectively, I needed to see how the N.M.A.H. had marked the 1976 Bicentennial, when the museum, the Smithsonian, and the federal government were all helmed by white men.

To my surprise, there was nary an exhibition dedicated to a Founding Father. But there had been a monumental show called “The Nation of Nations,” whose subject was America’s diversity. It opened with a survey of Native cultures, tracing the country’s identity as a “nation of immigrants” to the first Siberians who crossed the Bering Strait. A display about Ellis Island—which played recordings in dozens of languages—celebrated modern immigration, while a re-created nineteenth-century classroom was used to explain the process of naturalization. An entire section dedicated to American prejudice included anti-Japanese signage and a Ku Klux Klan hood.

Curators seem not to have worried that this would divide the American people. In the exhibition catalogue, then secretary of the Smithsonian S. Dillon Ripley—a former intelligence officer who was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by Ronald Reagan—describes America as “a place of turmoil among red men, white men, black men, and yellow men.” Yet no one hauled him before Congress to answer for stoking racial tensions, snubbing George Washington, or making America sad on her birthday. Today’s Smithsonian should be equally uncontroversial—and, without the Trump Administration’s propaganda, it probably would be.

The institution remains vulnerable. Republicans have proposed cutting its budget by more than ten per cent, and if they can fill the vacancies on its Board of Regents before the midterm elections, they may be able to fire Bunch. Yet there are also signs that the right’s revisionism panic might be petering out. Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska recently came out in support of the Smithsonian, while the Second Lady, Usha Vance, even feels comfortable collaborating with it. In May, she led a story-time event at the N.M.A.H. in honor of Asian American and Pacific Islander Heritage Month—in other words, a D.E.I. event for children, at a museum that her party believes is full of “inappropriate sexual and ideological content.” (She read from “Masala Chai, Fast and Slow,” by Rajani LaRocca, who is also known for “Some of Us,” a book for early readers that celebrates immigrant citizenship.)

She’s not the only conservative who didn’t get the memo. The day after my visit to the N.M.A.H., I went to see “America’s Presidents” at the National Portrait Gallery, where I found a father and son snapping selfies in front of Trump’s glowering mien. “We wanted to have a last weekend together before he went off to college,” the man explained; earlier, they’d been to the National Air and Space Museum. The man proudly acknowledged supporting Trump, but seemed confused when I asked if he’d spotted anything “radical.” He recalled a caption about a “wealthy landowner back in the day” who’d enslaved Native Americans, which he wasn’t sure was relevant, but he wouldn’t go so far as to say that it ought to be removed. “I don’t know if it’s unpatriotic,” he said. “It’s all good and bad. It’s part of our history.” ♦
